3:40 PM
For example: CAV and CLV (and CAA I guess but that's pretty much just more efficient CLV) are two different methods that an optical disc can be read. CAV keeps the disc spinning at a constant velocity no matter where the laser is, while CLV slows down the disc if it's near the edge and speeds it up near the center, allowing for more efficient disc usage. Both methods of disc reading have their advantages for certain use cases. For example, CLV is better for media playback with limited interactivity since it's more efficient with little drawback, while CAV is better for more interactive use cases like video games since loading times are reduced from the disc not needing to change speed.
3:41 PM
UMD, however, was used both for movie playback AND game playback. Did it use CLV for video and CAV for games, or did it stick to one method of disc spinning for every use case?
3:42 PM
This should be an easy question to get the answer to, because all ya gotta do is watch the disc while it's spinning and notice if the speed changes. However, the UMD is hidden from sight when in use, and it's small enough that it's kinda hard to tell.
3:43 PM
So I went to google to get a straight answer. For some reason, nobody has documented this. Which is extremely annoying.
3:44 PM
I'm going to assume it uses CLV for everything for now, since the specifications are not too far off from DVD except in a smaller form factor, so the speed changes shouldn't be too much of a hinderance.
3:46 PM
(The distance between the data is 0.04 micrometers closer on UMD, going from 0.74 μm to 0.70, and the laser wavelength is 10 nanometers longer with UMD compared to DVD, going from 650 nm to 660. Aside from that, they're shockingly close.) (edited)
3:50 PM
It still is kinda shocking a disc a small fraction of the size of DVD can still hold about 20% of the data while maintaining most of the same specs though.
3:51 PM
Especially considering it's a disc from 2004. Two years before HD-DVD and Blu-Ray would hit the mainstream consumer market.

Sorta the predecessor for the UMD, it was a music in a tiny form factor that was most popular in Japan, but did gain a small amount of traction in Europe, though it was a total flop in North America.
4:22 PM
It was smaller than a cassette walkman but could hold a CD's worth of music, albiet compressed. You could also rewrite the discs, like a casette. Until the rise of MP3 players, it was a solid option for portable music playback, and in Japan you were even able to rip CDs onto Minidiscs from a PS2.

4:36 PM
...but I'll tell you anyway this: -Vinyl records, CED, and VHD are CAV. They use a stylus instead of a laser, but as disc-based media, they still count for this. -Dreamcast, OG Xbox, Gamecube, and Wii all also use CAV, to reduce loading times. This may explain why load times were often substantially longer on PS2 compared to other 6th gen consoles. -CD-Audio, Video CD, DVD-Video, and Blu-Ray are all CLV. Most optical-disc-based consoles 7th gen and later are also usually CLV.

LAST TIME ON DRAGON BALL Z: After the team’s unanimous voteout of Scaredy, we were thrusted into a challenge to make a patron. We were immediately hit with butting heads, with Wendi wanting it to strictly be a God, me wanting to be more free with it and focus more on the abilities, and nobody having any strong vision. We ended up trying to theme it around envy, but even I could tell the theming was being barely kept together with ear wax and toothpicks. The final result? A sloppy and misguided OC with some cool ideas but just as much confusion, with a fittingly low score. Now’s the part where I need to act cordial, even if I don’t feel so. Typo, seeming beginning to feel their outsider status in the tribe, used their Mulan ability to give us another shot. We scrapped it all from the core and started over. I suggested an old ability idea of making sure two people always remained in the same realm, which evolved into the idea of arranged marriages as a gameplay mechanic, which evolved into making a Newlyweds Game format change. From there, we settled on a close-enough area of devotion/marriage. We made a Patron based off of that which deserved at least 55%, but we seemingly interrupted the judges weekly drug binge, which is a mistake I apologize for in hindsight, because I completely understand that it’s a bit of a dick move to do that. What’s not understandable is the grade they gave us, because they graded us worse for doing the same structure as last time, despite this submission merely replacing the last one. I could go on for a few more books, but I’d want to make money off those. In the background, the vote for “just in case” became evident. Typo had to be the one, they’d be the most comfortable tooth to pull and apparently fed some bad information to the team at one point. 6:42 PM
Whelp, in that case, allow me to just have a hyperfixated rant about Mega Man X rereleases
6:43 PM
So, you might remember the image where I said I was playing “The PS2 port of the PS1 port of the SNES version of Mega Man X3”
6:43 PM
Well, you may be asking (no you aren’t) “Why this emulated PS2 version? Why not the original?”
6:44 PM
Well, first off, this is why not the original:
6:45 PM
Mega Man X2 and especially X3 are stupidly expensive in the US, and even more in Europe. (Though the Japanese versions are much cheaper, I think 30 bucks each)
6:47 PM
Both X2 and X3 used a special chip in the cartridge called the Cx4 chip, which made them more expensive. Additionally, X3 was a very late release in the US, coming out in ‘96, the same year as the N64.
6:47 PM
But why not play the 32-bit versions? It was released on both the Sega Saturn and the PS1!
6:47 PM
…in Japan and Europe.
6:49 PM
Yeah, we didn’t get either version in the US. IDK why not the Saturn, but the PlayStation had a rule for its first few years outright banning completely 2D games like X3. Funny enough, it would be Mega Man 8 and X4 that would break this policy in ‘97. Capcom was just like “Aight, if you don’t want it we’ll just make these games Saturn exclusive in the US”. And that was enough to change Sony of America’s policy.
6:50 PM
I mean, the Saturn was popular in Japan and Capcom primarily dealt there, they could afford to skip out on American success.
6:51 PM
But here’s the fun thing about the PS2 version: It’s based off the PS1 version… but was American exclusive.
6:51 PM
Like, not even in Europe. The Mega Man X Collection was US only. And it’s the best way to play most of the games, since unlike the later collection, every game on it was natively ported.
6:52 PM
Which means the SNES games no longer have slowdown, and the PS1 games have almost no load times.
6:52 PM
Additionally, the collection is one of the few PS2 games that runs in 240p, so the games look extremely sharp on a CRT.
6:53 PM
(The Gamecube version is one of only TWO games on that platform that runs in 240p as well, fun fact)
6:54 PM
…so why not play the 2018 Mega Man X Legacy Collection?
6:55 PM
For some reason, -X3 is based off the SNES version, slowdown and all. -The input delay is very noticeable and very annoying. These games need fast response times and the lag makes that impossible.
6:56 PM
Funny enough though, X7 and X8 WERE natively ported in the X Legacy Collection. Hurray. X7 was natively ported. Quite possibly the worst Mega Man game in the series.
6:57 PM
IDK I just wanted to yap. Even if the X Legacy Collection is your only option, still play the Mega Man X games.
6:57 PM
They’re* really good. (X1, X2, X4, and X8 are good. X3 and X5 are okay, and X6 and X7 are terrible.)
